questions.q: What is cloud computing?
options: Software that only runs on one office server
The delivery of pay-as-you-go computing services hosted on infrastructure over the internet
A backup of your files on a USB drive
questions.explain: Cloud services (storage, databases, networking, analytics…) are rented over the internet and paid for as you use them.
questions.evidence: The Cloud, or Cloud Computing, is the delivery of a wide range of pay-as-you-go computing services hosted on an infrastructure over the internet.

questions.q: A private cloud refers to computing resources that are…
options: used exclusively by a single business or organization
shared by many companies over the public internet
provided free of charge by governments
questions.explain: A private cloud is dedicated to one organisation and runs on a private network.
questions.evidence: Private cloud: refers to cloud computing resources used exclusively by a single business or organization

questions.q: What is a software dependency?
options: A bug that only appears in production
A relationship where one software component relies on another to work properly
A container that has stopped running
questions.explain: Conflicting or missing dependencies are a classic installation problem that containers help solve.
questions.evidence: A software dependency is a relationship between software components where one component relies on the other to work properly.

questions.q: What is a container image?
options: A running instance of an application
A screenshot of a server's desktop
An account on a container registry
The template from which particular containers are created
questions.explain: Images are templates; containers are running (or stopped) instances created from them.
questions.evidence: a container image is the template from which particular instances of containers will be created

questions.q: What is Docker Hub?
options: An online repository of container images
A command that deletes old containers
questions.explain: Registries such as Docker Hub and quay.io host images you can pull and reuse.
questions.evidence: The Docker Hub is an online repository of container images, a vast number of which are publicly available.

questions.q: What is a Dockerfile?
options: A log of every container you have run
A plain text file with keywords and commands used to create a new container image
A compressed copy of a container
questions.explain: Writing the build steps in a Dockerfile makes images reproducible, unlike snapshotting an interactive session.
questions.evidence: A Dockerfile is a plain text file with keywords and commands that can be used to create a new container image.

questions.q: What does version control mean?
options: Locking files so only one person can edit them
Keeping track of changes to your code over time
Checking which software versions users have installed
questions.explain: Version control records every change, with clear commit messages explaining why.
questions.evidence: Version control means keeping track of changes to your code over time.

questions.q: Why run automated tests every time you make a change?
options: It removes the need for user research
It makes deployments slower but safer
questions.explain: Fast feedback from continuous integration means problems are caught and fixed early.
questions.evidence: By testing your code automatically every time you make a change, you’ll be able to find defects more quickly.

questions.q: What is external monitoring?
options: Monitoring memory use inside your servers
Monitoring set up outside your service that keeps checking it even if your infrastructure goes down
questions.explain: Internal monitoring watches metrics inside your infrastructure; external monitoring still works when that infrastructure fails.
questions.evidence: External monitoring is the monitoring you should set up outside of your service which keeps checking your systems even if your infrastructure goes down.

questions.q: To maximise uptime, how many states should your service be designed to have?
options: More possible states than simply ‘on’ or ‘off’
It doesn't matter as long as you have backups
questions.explain: Graceful degradation (for example read-only modes) keeps a service useful when parts of it fail.
questions.evidence: Your service should have more possible states than simply ‘on’ or ‘off’.

questions.q: Under the UK government's Cloud First policy, what must you do before considering other hosting options?
options: Ask users which host they prefer
Consider and fully evaluate public cloud solutions
Pick the cheapest supplier straight away
questions.explain: Public cloud is the default; other options need justification.
questions.evidence: You must consider and fully evaluate public cloud solutions before considering other options

questions.q: Which costs should you weigh when deciding how to host a service?
options: Operational costs over the service's expected lifetime, and the value of flexibility
questions.explain: Hosting is a long-term decision; flexibility has value too.
questions.evidence: You should consider the operational costs for the expected lifetime of your service and the value of flexibility.

questions.q: Containers are an example of what?
questions.explain: A container behaves like a second virtual computer running on a host.
questions.evidence: Containers are an example of what's called virtualization

questions.q: Like shipping containers, what do software containers make possible?
options: Running software without any operating system
Dropping a complete software system onto any computer with container software, where it should just work
Making every program run faster than natively
Never having to install any software again
questions.explain: Containers package software and its dependencies in a standard way.
questions.evidence: you can drop a container into any computer with the container software installed

questions.q: Which Podman command is used to interact with container images?
questions.explain: Its subcommands list, pull and remove images.
questions.evidence: The podman image command is used to interact with Podman container images.

questions.q: How can you stop finished containers from piling up on your computer?
options: Add the --rm flag to podman container run
questions.explain: --rm removes the container automatically when it exits.
questions.evidence: add the --rm flag to podman container run

questions.q: If Podman pulls the hello-world image with no further information, where does it come from?
questions.explain: Registries such as Docker Hub and quay.io host container images.
questions.evidence: it will be retrieved from Quay

questions.q: Why build a container image from a Dockerfile instead of snapshotting changes made interactively?
options: Snapshots are not allowed by Podman
A Dockerfile is a reproducible recipe
questions.explain: Snapshotting works but is not easily reproducible.
questions.evidence: create our container image from a reproducible recipe, known as a Dockerfile

questions.q: In a Dockerfile, what does the CMD line specify?
options: The default command a container runs if no other command is given
The base image to start from
The files to copy into the image
questions.explain: FROM gives the base image; RUN installs software; CMD sets the default command.
questions.evidence: indicates the default command we want a container based on this container image to run, if no other command is provided

questions.q: What does the first line of the example Dockerfile (FROM) provide?
options: The command to run at start-up
The base container image to start from
questions.explain: Every image builds on top of an existing base image.
questions.evidence: container image we are going to start from

questions.q: Where should you keep all your build artifacts?
questions.explain: A central store means the artifact you tested is the one you deploy.
questions.evidence: You should keep all your artifacts in a central repository.

questions.q: Why have multiple deployment environments?
options: So every developer has their own production
To phase the rollout and make sure the software is adequately tested
questions.explain: A version reaches later environments only after passing earlier ones.
questions.evidence: You should have multiple deployment environments so you can phase the rollout of your software

questions.q: Where does GOV.UK deploy new software first?
questions.explain: Staging gives confidence the software works before production.
questions.evidence: GOV.UK deploys to its staging environment first

questions.q: What is one benefit of deployments that can happen during the normal working day?
options: Staff do not have to work unsociable hours
questions.explain: Frequent, low-risk releases don't need to be scheduled for nights or weekends.
questions.evidence: These can take place during the normal business day, which means staff do not have to work unsociable hours.

questions.q: What is 'infrastructure as code'?
options: Editing application code directly on servers
Using code to describe configuration and software dependencies
questions.explain: Infrastructure code can be tested, reused and documented like any other code.
questions.evidence: One way you can manage configuration is by using code to describe the configuration and software dependencies.

questions.q: How do you avoid code that works on the developers' machines but fails in production?
options: Use the same tools for development and production environments
Use different databases to compare results
questions.explain: Differences in software, databases or application servers cause these failures.
questions.evidence: Avoid this problem by using the same tools for your development and production environments.

questions.q: What does internal monitoring give you?
options: Real-time updates on metrics like memory use, page load times and network traffic
Checks that keep running when your infrastructure is down
questions.explain: External monitoring complements it by checking from outside your service.
questions.evidence: Internal monitoring is the monitoring you should set up inside your infrastructure and will give you real time updates about metrics like memory usage, page load times, and network traffic.

questions.q: By which phase must a government service have monitoring in place?
questions.explain: During alpha the team agrees what and how to monitor.
questions.evidence: By the time you reach public beta, you must have monitoring in place for your service

questions.q: Why must you understand your service's dependencies, and theirs?
options: Your uptime depends on the availability of many systems, possibly from several suppliers
questions.explain: Each dependency's uptime expectations limit your own.
questions.evidence: Your service depends on the availability of many systems

questions.q: When may a government team choose an alternative to the cloud?
options: Only if it can show the alternative is better value for money
If the alternative is more modern
questions.explain: The case is made in service assessments or spending assurance.
questions.evidence: You can only choose an alternative to the cloud if you can show it

questions.q: What should you use to evaluate cloud providers' security?
questions.explain: NCSC cloud security guidance also helps decide if a provider meets your needs.
questions.evidence: Cloud Security Principles to help you evaluate cloud providers
